title: No Translation-Invariant Measure in Infinite Dimensions
description: Proves that no nonzero translation-invariant σ-finite Borel measure exists on an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space. The orthonormal separation argument: infinitely many disjoint equal-measure balls inside a bounded region force each ball's measure to 0.

meta.author: Gross (1967), Wiener
originalContributions: Pairwise disjoint balls for orthonormal families (proved)
Counting lemma: infinitely many equal-measure disjoint sets in finite-measure set → measure 0 (proved)
Translation invariance implies equal ball measures (proved)
Main impossibility: translation-invariant measure with finite bounded sets → all balls measure 0 (proved)
Small balls: μ(B(y, r)) = 0 for r ≤ 1/3, any center y (proved)
Parametric: μ(B(0, δ)) = 0 for any 0 < δ < √2/2 with μ(B(0, 1+δ)) < ∞ (proved)

overview.historicalContext: The impossibility of constructing a translation-invariant, $\sigma$-finite measure on infinite-dimensional spaces was recognized as a fundamental obstacle in functional analysis by the mid-20th century. Norbert Wiener's construction of Brownian motion (1923) implicitly required measures on function spaces, but Wiener measure is not translation-invariant — shifting a Brownian path changes its law. Leonard Gross's 1967 paper 'Abstract Wiener Spaces' gave the definitive framework: Gaussian measures live naturally on the Banach completion of a Hilbert space, not on the Hilbert space itself. The impossibility proof in this formalization — using orthonormal separation to pack infinitely many equal-measure disjoint balls into a bounded region — is the standard argument appearing in textbooks by Reed-Simon, Brezis, and others. It demonstrates a fundamental dichotomy: $\mathbb{R}^n$ admits Lebesgue measure because finite-dimensional balls have finite packing density, but infinite-dimensional spaces do not.
overview.problemStatement: Can a nonzero translation-invariant σ-finite Borel measure exist on an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space? **No.** Given an orthonormal sequence $\{e_n\}$, the balls $B(e_n, 1/3)$ are pairwise disjoint (since $\|e_n - e_m\| = \sqrt{2} > 2/3$), all contained in $B(0, 4/3)$, and all have equal measure by translation invariance. Since $\mu(B(0, 4/3)) < \infty$, each ball has measure 0. By translation invariance, every ball has measure 0, so $\mu = 0$.
overview.text: Formalizes the full impossibility argument in Lean 4. Proves: orthonormal family separation (√2), pairwise disjoint balls, containment in bounded region, the key counting lemma (∞ equal-measure disjoint sets in finite set → measure 0), translation-invariant balls have equal measure, and the main theorem combining all ingredients.
overview.proofStrategy: 1. Prove orthonormal_family_dist: any two distinct members of an orthonormal family are √2 apart. 2. Prove orthonormal_balls_pairwise_disjoint: balls of radius 1/3 are pairwise disjoint. 3. Prove orthonormal_ball_subset_bounded: each ball is in B(0, 4/3). 4. Prove measure_eq_zero_of_disjoint_infinite: the key counting lemma via ENNReal.tsum_const_eq_top_of_ne_zero. 5. Prove translation_invariant_balls_eq: translation invariance gives equal ball measures. 6. Combine all for no_translation_invariant_measure.
keyInsights: The counting lemma is the heart: if ∑_{n=0}^∞ c = ⊤ for c > 0 (a constant series), but the union of disjoint sets has finite measure, then c = 0. This uses ENNReal.tsum_const_eq_top_of_ne_zero from Mathlib.
The orthonormal separation √2 > 2/3 is crucial but the exact threshold is unimportant — any radius r < √2/2 works. We use r = 1/3 for concreteness.
The containment B(eₙ, 1/3) ⊆ B(0, 4/3) follows from triangle inequality and ‖eₙ‖ = 1.
Translation invariance means μ(A + v) = μ(A), which makes all balls of a given radius have the same measure. Combined with the counting lemma, this forces μ(B(x, 1/3)) = 0 for all x.
The argument is purely geometric and works for any infinite-dimensional space admitting an orthonormal sequence — no special structure beyond inner product space is needed.

sections.title: §1: Orthonormal Separation
sections.summary: Proves orthonormal vectors are √2 apart and balls of radius 1/3 are disjoint.
sections.mathContext: For orthonormal $e_i, e_j$ with $i \neq j$: $\|e_i - e_j\|^2 = \|e_i\|^2 - 2\langle e_i, e_j\rangle + \|e_j\|^2 = 2$. Since $\sqrt{2} > 2/3$, balls $B(e_i, 1/3) \cap B(e_j, 1/3) = \emptyset$.

sections.title: §2: Pairwise Disjoint Ball Family
sections.summary: Lifts the pairwise separation to a full Pairwise Disjoint statement for the ball family indexed by ℕ.
sections.mathContext: The family $\{B(e_n, 1/3)\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is pairwise disjoint: for $i \neq j$, $\|e_i - e_j\| = \sqrt{2} > 2 \cdot 1/3$.

sections.title: §3: Containment in Bounded Region
sections.summary: Each ball B(eₙ, 1/3) ⊆ B(0, 4/3) via triangle inequality.

sections.title: §4: Counting Lemma and Infrastructure
sections.summary: The key measure-theoretic lemmas: translation-invariant definition, equal ball measures, OrthoSeq structure, ball containment, and pairwise disjoint balls from orthonormal separation.
sections.mathContext: If $\mu(S) < \infty$ and $s_n \subseteq S$ are pairwise disjoint with $\mu(s_n) = c$ for all $n$, then $c \cdot \aleph_0 = \sum_n c \leq \mu(S) < \infty$, so $c = 0$. Applied to $s_n = B(e_n, 1/3)$ and $S = B(0, 4/3)$.

sections.title: §5: Main Impossibility Theorem and Corollary
sections.summary: no_invariant_locally_finite_ball assembles all ingredients to prove μ(B(0, 1/3)) = 0. Corollary: μ(B(y, 1/3)) = 0 for any center y.
sections.mathContext: $\mu(B(0, 1/3)) = 0$ follows from zero_measure_of_infinite_disjoint applied to the orthonormal ball family. Corollary: $\mu(B(y, 1/3)) = \mu(B(0, 1/3)) = 0$ for all $y \in H$ by translation invariance.

sections.title: §6–7: Small Balls and Parametric Extension
sections.summary: Extends impossibility: μ(B(y, r)) = 0 for any r ≤ 1/3 (monotone containment), and parametrically μ(B(0, δ)) = 0 for any 0 < δ < √2/2.
sections.mathContext: Part VI: $B(y, r) \subseteq B(y, 1/3)$ for $r \leq 1/3$, so $\mu(B(y, r)) \leq \mu(B(y, 1/3)) = 0$. Part VII: any $\delta$ with $2\delta < \sqrt{2}$ makes the orthonormal balls $B(e_n, \delta)$ pairwise disjoint and contained in $B(0, 1+\delta)$, with the same counting argument giving $\mu(B(0,\delta)) = 0$.

conclusion.summary: No nonzero translation-invariant σ-finite Borel measure exists on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. The proof combines orthonormal separation (√2), pairwise disjoint balls, bounded containment, the counting lemma for infinite equal-measure families, and translation invariance. Fully proved for balls of radius 1/3 and extended parametrically to all radii 0 < δ < √2/2.
openQuestions: Can this be strengthened to show μ = 0 as a measure (not just zero on balls)? Needs countable covering of open sets (Lindelöf property).
Can Gaussian measures on abstract Wiener spaces be formalized as the constructive replacement?
conclusion.implications: This result explains why infinite-dimensional analysis requires fundamentally different measure theory. Gaussian measures (Wiener, path integrals) replace Lebesgue measure, living on Banach completions rather than Hilbert spaces.

crossReferences.description: Extends the orthonormal separation from OQ-03 to the full impossibility theorem
